en: What it shows: Simple rules alone, "two chemicals that spread and react," make spots, stripes, labyrinths and coral appear by themselves, with nobody drawing them. The rules are identical in every cell, yet the patterns are completely different, and two numbers like the feed rate F and kill rate k create that difference. In this implementation the spots settle as about 50 separate dots, while stripes and coral settle as a single connected shape.

What it doesn't show: It is not proof that real zebra stripes form through this reaction. Real animal patterns involve many more factors such as gene activity, body growth and body shape, and F and k here are mathematical settings, not biological values. The "mitosis" setting ended up with nearly the same shape as spots on a grid this size, and not every process its name suggests is visible.

An implementation inspired by the idea of Turing (1952, "The chemical basis of morphogenesis", Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 237) and by the Gray–Scott patterns shown by Pearson (1993, "Complex patterns in a simple system", Science 261). It does not reproduce the paper's figures exactly.

Equations: du = 0.16·lap(u) − u·v² + F(1 − u), dv = 0.08·lap(v) + u·v² − (F + k)·v. Each step uses dt = 1, the Laplacian is computed from the four neighbors, and the edges wrap around. One step on screen is 40 calculations. The diffusion coefficients differ from Pearson's, so the shapes are not identical.

The four presets (F, k) are spots (0.035, 0.065), stripes (0.029, 0.057), mitosis (0.0367, 0.0649) and coral (0.0545, 0.062). Running 3 seeds for 20,000 iterations, all values stayed finite, and the area covered by the pattern was about 19% for spots, 21% for mitosis, 43% for stripes and 53% for coral. The number of blobs was around 50 for spots and mitosis and 1 (one connected shape) for stripes and coral (verify with node tools/validate-turing.js).
The number of iterations for the pattern to settle was about 2,000 for stripes, about 6,000 for coral and about 12,000 for spots and mitosis. The screen runs up to 30,000 iterations.
The code is available on GitHub.
Which Society Would You Choose Behind the Veil of Ignorance? · Simulatio Lab
If you did not know where in society you would be born, which society would you choose? Run the Rawls and Harsanyi thought experiment while changing how risk-averse people are.

If you did not know whether you would be born rich or poor, which society would you pick? The philosopher Rawls argued that rules chosen behind such a "veil of ignorance" are fair. But even for the same question, the answer depends on how much you dislike risk. Follow that fork in the road with numbers.

There are five candidate societies. Each fixes an income for each of five positions (the population split into fifths by income; position 1 is the poorest). We assume that the more equal a society is, the lower its average income. That assumption drives the results.

A citizen behind the veil does not know which position they will occupy. One of the five positions is assigned with equal probability (this is Harsanyi's assumption; Rawls held that such probabilities cannot be known).

In the expected-utility rule, the utility of income y is y1−γ/(1−γ) (log when γ = 1), and people choose the society with the highest expected utility. γ is how much they dislike risk. At γ = 0 only the average income matters; as γ grows the poorest position counts for more.

For comparison there are two pure rules: maximize the average (close to utilitarianism) and maximize the minimum (close to Rawls's difference principle: the society where the poorest position earns the most).

What it shows: With these five societies and income numbers, the choice changes step by step with risk aversion γ. Below γ = 0.7 the winner-take-all lottery society was chosen; from 0.7 up to 1.0 the steep-pyramid society; from 1.0 up to 2.15 the mild-gap society; from 2.15 up to 6.1 the safety-net society; and at 6.1 or more the equal society. Maximizing the average chose the lottery society and maximizing the minimum chose the equal society. With a group average γ of 2 and spread of 1, out of 1,000 people about 44–46% chose the safety-net society, about 38% the mild-gap society, about 11% the winner-take-all lottery society and about 5–6% the steep-pyramid society (two seeds). Even behind the same veil, what counts as the "fair choice" can change with how people treat risk.
